label: Saying No
framing: A no you mean is worth more than a yes you resent. Scripture does not praise the man who carries everything, but the one who knows his limits, keeps his word, and does not let his speech swell beyond what he can deliver. To say no clearly is to honor the yes you have already given.
cultural: The ancient world ran on the household and the patron, where a request from above was hard to refuse and obligation was the air people breathed. Even there, Jesus withdrew from the crowds that wanted him, and did not heal every sick person in Galilee before he prayed. He was not ruled by the urgency of the nearest demand. We are, and we call it kindness, when often it is fear of being thought small.
historical: The desert fathers of the fourth century fled the noise of the city precisely to learn what one life could and could not hold. Centuries later the Reformers recovered the goodness of vocation, a particular calling with a particular shape, against the idea that the holy life meant taking on every duty. Eugene Peterson, writing in our own time, warned pastors that a packed calendar is often vanity wearing the mask of service.
application: Decide your yes before the request comes, so the answer is already shaped by your calling and not by the pressure in the room. Let your no be plain and kind, without the long apology that invites argument. Notice when you say yes to be liked, and confess it, because that is not love, it is fear. And protect the few things you are actually called to by refusing the many you are not.

verses.text: And He said to them, “Come with Me privately to a solitary place, and let us rest for a while.” For many people were coming and going, and they did not even have time to eat.
verses.where: When the apostles come back from their mission, Jesus invites them to come away to a solitary place and rest, because so many people are coming and going that they have no time even to eat. The site's plain note adds what happens next: the crowd arrives anyway, and Jesus sees sheep without a shepherd and teaches them. Rest is commanded, and love still decides when it gives way; both belong to the same day.

verses.text: So the Twelve summoned all the disciples and said, “It is unacceptable for us to neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables. Therefore, brothers, select from among you seven men confirmed to be full of the Spirit and wisdom. We will appoint this responsibility to them and will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.”
verses.where: When widows are being overlooked in the daily food distribution, the Twelve say it is not right for them to neglect the word of God to wait on tables, and they have the community choose seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom for the work. The site's plain note says they did not treat practical service as less spiritual than prayer and preaching. Their no to one good work was a yes to their own calling and to other people's gifts.

verses.text: Which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost to see if he has the resources to complete it? Otherwise, if he lays the foundation and is unable to finish the work, everyone who sees it will ridicule him, saying, ‘This man could not finish what he started to build.’
verses.where: Jesus asks who would start building a tower without first sitting down to count the cost. The site's note says building on a grand scale was a mark of status in Herodian Palestine, and an unfinished project was an obvious public embarrassment. Jesus is speaking of the cost of following him, and the picture holds for any yes: count it before you give it.

verses.text: It is a trap for a man to dedicate something rashly, only later to reconsider his vows.
verses.where: A proverb calls it a trap to dedicate something rashly and only afterward reconsider the vow. The site's note lists rash vows among the daily matters the chapter covers. A hasty yes, given to escape an awkward moment, can bind a person to something they never weighed.

verses.text: When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it, because He takes no pleasure in fools. Fulfill your vow. It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it.
verses.where: The Teacher tells those who come before God to listen more than they speak and to keep their vows, and says it is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill it. The site's note on the chapter gathers this counsel under how a person should come before God. An honest no is better than a promise that will be broken.

verses.text: Then Jesus, realizing that they were about to come and make Him king by force, withdrew again to a mountain by Himself.
verses.where: After the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus realizes the crowd means to make him king by force, and he withdraws to the hills alone. The site's plain note says they wanted the wrong kind of king, and that it is possible to want Jesus very much and still want him on our own terms. He said no to a role the crowd was eager to give him, because it was not the one his Father had given.

verses.text: But Daniel made up his mind that he would not defile himself with the king’s food or wine. So he asked the chief official for permission not to defile himself.
verses.where: Daniel, a young captive trained for the king's service, resolves not to defile himself with the king's food and wine, and he asks the chief official for permission rather than defying him. The site's note on the chapter tells of the ten-day test he proposes. A no can be firm and respectful at the same time, and can come with a way forward.

verses.text: For if the eagerness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what he does not have.
verses.where: Urging the Corinthians to finish their collection for the believers in Jerusalem, Paul says a gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one does not have. The site's plain note says Paul does not order them to give, and asks the reader to give from what Christ has given rather than from guilt or from what others give. God does not ask for what a person does not have.

verses.text: Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain; unless the LORD protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain. In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for bread to eat— for He gives sleep to His beloved.
verses.where: The song says that building and guarding are in vain unless the LORD builds and guards, and that it is in vain to rise early and stay up late, for he gives sleep to his beloved. The site's plain note says the psalm does not tell anyone to stop working; it says that worry is not the same as work, and that lying down to rest can be an act of trust. Not everything depends on you.

verses.text: To everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:
verses.where: The Teacher's poem lists fourteen pairs of opposites, as the site's note puts it: a time to keep and a time to discard, a time to be silent and a time to speak. A life with a time for everything is not a life with time for everything at once. Choosing one season's work means letting another wait.

related.label: People-Pleasing and the Fear of Man

misread.taken: Jesus' words to Martha are often read as a ranking, prayer above work and quiet people above busy ones, so that those who keep everything running hear only a rebuke, and are then asked to do all of it and sit still too.
misread.says: The site's plain note says Luke does not set it up that way. Just before, Jesus told the lawyer to go and do like the Samaritan, and he called himself one who serves. The trouble was not that Martha served; it was that she served anxious and resentful, and wanted Jesus to take her sister from his feet. The note says Jesus is not scolding the one who carries the load: he sees how much she carries and says her name with love. Part of hearing him may be letting some of the preparations go undone.
misread.text: “Martha, Martha,” the Lord replied, “you are worried and upset about many things. But only one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, and it will not be taken away from her.”

whole: Many people who cannot say no are not lazy or weak. They are capable, and that is the problem: they are asked for everything. They sit on three committees, run the school fundraiser, cover a colleague's shift, host the family holidays, answer every message, and lie awake making lists. Some say yes because they are afraid of disappointing someone. Some say yes because it is good work and they cannot see how to refuse a good thing. Some have been taught that a Christian should never turn down a request from church. The result is often a life spread so thin that nothing is done well, the people closest to them get what is left over, and the yes they give with their mouth is resented in their heart.

Scripture is plainer about limits than we often are. Jesus told his tired friends to come away and rest, and he withdrew when a crowd tried to make him king. The apostles said it was not right for them to leave their calling to wait on tables, and they gave that good work to others who were gifted for it. Proverbs calls a rash vow a trap, and Ecclesiastes says it is better not to vow than to vow and fail to keep it. Paul says a gift is measured by what a person has, not by what they do not have. Behind many of our yeses is something the Bible would call pride or fear: the belief that it all depends on us, or the dread of what people will think if we decline. Martha was serving Jesus and missing him at the same time, and most of us know that from the inside.

So the Bible's wisdom is to count the cost before saying yes, and to say no without shame. Ask what God has given you to do in this season, and let that shape your answers, as the apostles did. Give your yes freely when it is yours to give, and let it be a yes you will keep. When the answer is no, say it plainly and kindly; a long excuse is not required, and a respectful no can come with another way forward, as Daniel's did. Remember that every yes to one thing is a no to something else, often to rest, to prayer, or to the people at home. Sometimes love will interrupt the plan, as it did when the crowd found Jesus on the shore. But a person who never says no will sooner or later fail the people who most need them.

The hope Scripture gives is that the work is God's before it is ours. Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain, and he gives sleep to his beloved. Jesus left a town full of people looking for him to go where he was sent (Mark 1:38), and at the end he could pray that he had accomplished the work his Father gave him to do (John 17:4). The same freedom is offered to anyone who follows him: not to do everything, but to do what is given, and to trust God with the rest. A no spoken in that trust is not a failure of love. It is room made for the love that is actually yours to give.
deep.sit: What is one commitment you said yes to out of fear or habit rather than calling, and what would it take to lay it down well?

prayer.lead: A short song of a soul that has stopped reaching for what is too great for it. The site's plain note says it asks you to set down some of the questions and ambitions you have been grabbing at, and to be quiet with God while they wait.
prayer.text: My heart is not proud, O LORD, my eyes are not haughty. I do not aspire to great things or matters too lofty for me. Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul; like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me. O Israel, put your hope in the LORD, both now and forevermore.
